clue.text: Pay bill to dance — it's subject to inflation

definitions.note: a clause standing for the thing that is pumped up

parts.note: to foot the bill is to pay it, so 'pay bill' gives the verb meaning to settle up
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Someone settles the bill for a dance party, grumbling that prices keep rising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inflation' suggests economics, but the thing inflated is a ball pumped full of air.
explanation.definitionFit: A soccer or rugby ball is pumped with air through a valve before play.

clue.text: Succeed in parting

explanation.surface: Someone does well when leaving.
explanation.walkthrough: To fare well is to succeed; as one word it is the goodbye spoken on parting.
explanation.definitionFit: To fare well is to get on successfully; a farewell is a goodbye at a parting.

clue.text: Cancelled recent version as slightly unbalanced

parts.note: an event called off is cancelled

indicators.note: a new version of something is a reworking, so the letters of recent are rearranged

explanation.surface: A recent edition was withdrawn because it was a bit lopsided.
explanation.walkthrough: 'version' rearranges RECENT into CENTRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not quite in the middle is a little lopsided.

clue.text: Note rarely used reflexive English verb

indicators.note: reflexive suggests bending back on itself, so the letters are read in reverse

explanation.surface: A grammar note about an obscure English reflexive verb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reflexive' looks like grammar, but it turns E + VERB back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: A breve is a long note of two whole-note lengths, seldom seen in modern music.

clue.text: Catches girls without a ring

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the girls go round the ring

parts.note: lasses are girls
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: Someone snares young women who are not wearing a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking', but in its older sense means outside.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy lassoes cattle by roping them with a noose.

clue.text: Let down servicemen with clumsy lie

parts.note: ABs are able seamen, ratings in the Royal Navy

indicators.note: a clumsy lie is a badly made one, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Soldiers have disappointed someone by telling an awkward untruth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clumsy' rearranges LIE into EIL, placed after ABS.
explanation.definitionFit: To abseil is to lower oneself down a cliff or wall on a rope.

clue.text: Information may be found on it at the library

definitions.text: Information may be found on it at the library

parts.words: Information may be found on it at the library
parts.note: not an information desk but the shelving where volumes full of information stand

explanation.surface: Where to ask for help in a library.
explanation.definitionFit: Library volumes, which hold knowledge, are stored on these ledges.

clue.text: Register letter three times

parts.note: en is the name of the letter N
ter is Latin for three times, used on prescriptions

explanation.surface: Someone signs up by writing a letter three times over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letter' gives a letter's spelt-out name; TER (thrice) is familiar from the prescription abbreviation t.d.s.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter a competition or one's name in a list is to sign up for it.

clue.text: Provisional accommodation?

parts.note: read not as temporary housing but as a place that accommodates provisions

explanation.surface: Temporary housing.
explanation.definitionFit: A pantry is a room where food stores are kept.

clue.text: The cost of maintaining a mounted guard

parts.note: mounted means up on a horse
to keep is to guard or protect

explanation.surface: The expense of keeping a cavalry sentry on duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mounted guard' paints horse guards, but it splits as UP plus KEEP.
explanation.definitionFit: Upkeep is the expense of keeping property in good repair.

clue.text: Get sack from Winchester?

explanation.surface: Someone is dismissed from a job in the cathedral city of Winchester.
explanation.walkthrough: Winchester looks like the English city, but the question mark points to the Winchester repeating firearm.
explanation.definitionFit: To ransack or plunder a place is one sense; a Winchester is a famous make of long gun, the other.

clue.text: Patron evidently a royalist

explanation.surface: A wealthy sponsor turns out to favour the monarchy.
explanation.walkthrough: A royalist backs the crown, so is plainly one who holds it up.
explanation.definitionFit: A patron is a backer of a cause or artist; a royalist is a backer of the monarchy.

clue.text: Forlorn, getting distress order to quit

parts.note: woe is grief or distress
'begone!' is an old command telling someone to leave

explanation.surface: A person grows miserable after being told, in a troubling way, to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone forlorn looks sad and dejected, wearing a wretched expression.

clue.text: Minister to open play

explanation.surface: A clergyman is asked to start a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' looks like a noun for a clergyman or politician, but here it is a verb meaning to attend to.
explanation.definitionFit: To minister to someone is to wait on them; in tennis the first stroke that opens each point has the same name.

clue.text: Landlords of old billets?

explanation.surface: Property owners are described in terms of former soldiers' lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: Billets suggest quarters for troops, but 'billet' is also an old word for a short note.
explanation.definitionFit: Landlords are people who let property; billets were, in old usage, short written notes.

clue.text: Page one is free for work by spy

indicators.note: free letters are loosed and can be rearranged

explanation.surface: A spy is told the front page story will be released.
explanation.definitionFit: Espionage is the craft of secret agents gathering intelligence.

clue.text: Bogus form used in a public service

indicators.note: the reshuffled letters sit inside the public service

parts.note: PO stands for Post Office, a public service

indicators.note: to form something is to shape it anew, so the letters of used are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fake document is employed within a state department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form' rearranges USED into SEUD, which goes 'in' PO.
explanation.definitionFit: Pseudo means sham or not genuine, pretending to be something it is not.

clue.text: Love to dig out wild plant

indicators.note: out signals the letters being turned out of their order

explanation.surface: A gardener happily digs up a weed.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog violet is a common wild flower with scentless purple blooms.

clue.text: King coped with extremes of rivalry in science

parts.note: Geo is an abbreviation for George, a king's name
met, as in met a challenge, means coped with it

indicators.note: the extremes are the first and last letters of the word rivalry

explanation.surface: A king handled contending factions in the field of science.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Geometry is the mathematical study of shapes, lines and angles.

clue.text: Churchman dedicated to worship.

explanation.surface: A priest devotes his life to prayer.
explanation.walkthrough: William Temple and his father Frederick were both Archbishops of Canterbury; the second sense is a building consecrated for religious rites.
explanation.definitionFit: Temple was the surname of two Archbishops of Canterbury; a building set apart for divine worship is the other meaning.

clue.text: He was an Ironside before Cromwell

definitions.text: He was an Ironside before Cromwell

parts.words: He was an Ironside before Cromwell
parts.note: Ironsides was a nickname for Cromwell's cavalry, but an English king bore the epithet Ironside centuries earlier

explanation.surface: A soldier in Cromwell's army.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Cromwell's troops were the Ironsides; the king meant here reigned briefly in 1016, long before.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anglo-Saxon king who fought Cnut in 1016 was nicknamed Ironside.

clue.text: Safe house key for one on the run

parts.note: a refuge is a shelter or safe place
E is a musical key

explanation.surface: Someone fleeing seeks a hiding place and a key to get in.
explanation.definitionFit: A person fleeing persecution or war is an exile seeking shelter abroad.

clue.text: Dress foolishly, in a severe style

parts.note: to rig out is to dress
idly, in the sense of thoughtlessly or in vain

explanation.surface: Someone dresses foolishly in an austere way.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something strictly and inflexibly is doing it sternly.

clue.text: Have faith in unknown but well-behaved convict

parts.note: to trust is to have faith in
Y is a mathematical unknown

explanation.surface: We trust an obscure prisoner who has kept out of trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: A trusty is a prisoner given privileges for good conduct.

clue.text: A part to play — nothing more stirring

indicators.note: stirring mixes things up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: An actor says no role could be more exciting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stirring' looks like an adjective for an exciting role, but it rearranges O plus MORE.
explanation.definitionFit: Romeo is the title role in Shakespeare's tragedy, a part an actor plays.

clue.text: Less dash required here

explanation.surface: Less hurry is needed in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'dash' is the short horizontal stroke of the subtraction sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Less, as in seven less two, means take away; the subtraction sign is a short stroke.

clue.text: Greyfriars medium is master of such a force

parts.note: The Magnet was the boys' story paper in which the Greyfriars School tales of Billy Bunter appeared
M is an abbreviation for master, as in MA, Master of Arts

explanation.surface: A spiritualist at Greyfriars school commands mysterious powers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'medium' suggests a spiritualist, but it means the publication that carried the stories of Greyfriars, a fictional English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnetism is the attractive force exerted by iron and lodestone.

clue.text: Town noted for old sailors and classics

definitions.text: Town noted for old sailors and classics

parts.words: Town noted for old sailors and classics
parts.note: old sailors are salts, so a Surrey town known for its bath salts and for two classic flat races

explanation.surface: A naval port famous for sea dogs and Greek literature.
explanation.walkthrough: Old salts suggest sailors, but the salts are Epsom salts; the Derby and the Oaks, two of England's five classic horse races, are run on the downs there.
explanation.definitionFit: The Surrey town gave its name to magnesium sulphate salts and hosts the Derby.

clue.text: Brown belted William we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the spoken phrase gives the spelling entered

parts.note: William taken as a son, and belted meaning thrashed or tanned, gives a phrase like son tanned

explanation.surface: A boy called William wearing a brown belt.
explanation.walkthrough: William stands for a son, perhaps Just William, the schoolboy William Brown in Richmal Crompton's books; 'belted' means beaten, which is tanned.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin bronzed by exposure to sunshine has turned a darker shade.

clue.text: Opened up by the Adriatic

explanation.surface: Something was unlocked beside the Adriatic Sea.
explanation.walkthrough: Split is a port city on the Adriatic coast of Croatia.
explanation.definitionFit: Something cracked or burst apart has opened up; Split is a Croatian city on that sea.

clue.text: Those ready to please succeeded in the country

indicators.note: the abbreviation for succeeded is placed inside the country

parts.note: Yemen is a country in the Arabian peninsula
S is a standard abbreviation for succeeded, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: Eager-to-please people prospered in rural parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the country' looks like the countryside, but it is a specific country.
explanation.definitionFit: Sycophants who agree with whatever the boss says are eager to please.

clue.text: "Could frame thy fearful ?" (Blake)

parts.note: a gap to fill from the last line of the first verse of William Blake's poem The Tyger

explanation.surface: A line of Blake's poetry with its final word left blank.
explanation.definitionFit: Blake asks what immortal hand or eye could frame the tiger's fearful balance of form.
